[[Category:Set theory| 1]]
The '''cardinality''' of a set $S$, denoted $|S|$, is its number of elements. 

{{Hidden example}}
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! $S$
! | $|S|$
|-
| $\{1,2,3\}$
| 3
|-
| $\{a,b,c,\cdots,z\}$
| 26
|-
| $\{0,2,4,6,8,\cdots\}$
| $\infty$
|}
{{End hidden}}

<blockquote>
In everyday language, "size" is often used as an alternative term for cardinality.
</blockquote>

== Finity == 

<div class=center>
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! | $|S|$
! 
|-
| $<\infty$
| '''Finite set'''
|-
| $\infty$
| '''Infinite set'''
|}
</div>

== Countability ==

If

$$
\exists f:\mathbb{N} \to S
$$

then $S$ is said to be '''countable'''.

<blockquote>
All finite sets are countable. Infinite sets may be either countable (e.g., [[integer#Countability|$\mathbb{Z}$]]) or uncountable (e.g., [[real number|$\mathbb{R}$]]).
</blockquote>

=== Equipotence ===

If $|A|=|B|$, set $A,B$ are said to be '''equipotent''', denoted by $A\sim B$.
<ref>{{#cite:Q2196}}</ref>

== Cardinality of unions of sets ==

$$
\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} A_i\right|
= \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k+1}S_k
$$

where

$$
S_k = \sum_{1 \leq i_1 < \cdots < i_k \leq n}
|A_{i_1} \cap \cdots \cap A_{i_k}|
$$
